strengths: The motivation is clear and relevant. The analytical example demonstrates how context-free interventions and a fixed intervention scope can each exclude the optimal policy.

Combining existing POMPS characterization with contextual GP optimization and scope selection based on averaged optimistic values is a useful algorithmic direction. Separating scope-selection regret from action-selection regret helps explain the learning problem.

The experiments use 110 seeds, report uncertainty, and examine cases where competing methods can or cannot attain the same optimum. Noise, context-removal, and BO-backend ablations provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policies to the analyzed algorithm is not established. Definition 1 permits contexts downstream of some interventions and different information sets for different actions. Sections 3 and B.1 instead assume fixed context distributions followed by joint action selection. Grouping scopes solely by X(S) and C(S) also discards the individual C_X constraints. Consequently, the pointwise oracle max_x f_i(x,c) need not represent an admissible mixed policy. A restricted setting or a valid sequential reduction is needed.

The central regret guarantees contain substantive proof gaps. On page 27, action regret f_i^*(c) - f_i(x,c) is bounded by the range of f_i^* across contexts. That range can be zero while action regret is positive and context-dependent, so the stated martingale argument does not follow. Additionally, the instance-dependent proof concludes with worst-arm information gain through c(T), whereas Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 use the smaller averaged information gain in the leading term without justification.

The relationship between theory and implementation is insufficiently explained. The analysis assumes exact GP-UCB optimization, known independent GP priors, compact convex domains, and independent Gaussian observation noise. The experiments use HEBO with learned transformations, and several SCMs have unbounded Gaussian contexts or noise outside the assumed model. These experiments can demonstrate practical behavior, but they do not establish the claimed guarantees for the implemented procedure.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate the new contribution. Comparisons are limited to constructed SCMs and CaBO/CoBO baselines, often with policy classes that exclude the optimum by construction. The PSA experiments have only one POMPS and therefore do not test the proposed scope selector. Comparisons with Functional Causal BO and other applicable causal methods, plus alternative selectors operating over identical POMPSs, are missing. Backend and context ablations do not replace these comparisons.

The scalability claim is not demonstrated. Section 3 explicitly describes exponential brute-force scope enumeration. The large-variable experiment contains many redundant variables and few surviving scopes, but reports no enumeration runtime, memory usage, or scaling with the number of competing scopes. Reduced intervention counts therefore do not establish computational scalability.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing implementation details and inconsistent benchmark equations. Although a public implementation is claimed, the manuscript supplies no repository link or concrete experimental exploration schedules and kernel settings. Appendix A.1.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation before claiming to substitute it, and Appendix A.3 specifies C4 as depending on itself, contradicting the DAG. These errors leave the executable environments and some claimed optima ambiguous.
